--- title-block-style: none author: "" --- # Cohort Analysis :::: epigraph > It's almost impossible to get a really good understanding of a service's usage without looking at activity and retention numbers on a cohort-by-cohort basis. ::: {style="text-align: right"} — *Christoph Janz* ::: :::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ In [Chapter 3](Time%20Series%20Analysis.qmd) we explored time series analysis. Building on those methods, we now shift to a related approach with wide-ranging applications in business and beyond: cohort analysis. Cohort analysis is a branch of behavioral analytics that organizes data from a defined subset, such as a subscription service, online game, or retail platform, into meaningful groups rather than treating the dataset as a single unit. These groups, called cohorts, share common traits such as timing or scale. Dividing populations into cohorts and tracking them across time provides a powerful way to uncover differences among subgroups and observe how they evolve. This approach helps reduce bias and offers insights into long-term behavioral patterns. In this chapter, we will begin by clarifying what cohorts are and outlining the essential components of cohort analysis. After introducing the UK online store sales dataset used for examples, we will construct a retention analysis and address challenges such as defining cohorts and managing sparse data. We will then examine survivorship, returnship, and cumulative measures, which share structural similarities with retention analysis in Polars. Finally, we will explore how cohort analysis can be combined with cross-sectional methods to better understand population composition over time. ## Cohorts: A Useful Analysis Framework Before moving into the code, it is helpful to define cohorts, consider the kinds of questions they help answer, and review the elements of any cohort analysis. A *cohort* is a collection of entities that share a defining characteristic at the point when observation begins. While cohorts often consist of people, they can also include organizations, products, or natural phenomena. Members of a cohort may sometimes recognize their inclusion. For instance, athletes on the same sports team know they belong to that group, and employees hired in the same training program understand they are part of a shared intake. In other cases, cohorts are created virtually. A streaming service, for example, might group all subscribers who joined during a particular quarter to study how long they remain active. Whenever entities are grouped without their explicit awareness, it is important to consider the ethical implications, especially when different treatments or interventions are applied. *Cohort analysis* provides a structured way to compare groups over extended periods. Many behaviors unfold gradually over weeks, months, or years, and cohort analysis helps us interpret these trajectories. It offers a framework for identifying relationships between cohort attributes and long-term outcomes, which can inspire hypotheses about underlying causes. For example, customers who joined through a discount promotion may display different purchasing habits compared to those who discovered a brand organically. Monitoring new cohorts against historical ones can highlight early signals of success or potential problems. Cohort analysis also enables us to revisit historical data when controlled experiments are not possible. Although A/B testing, covered in [Chapter 7](link), remains the strongest method for establishing causality, cohort analysis is valuable for generating hypotheses and deepening our understanding of customer behavior. Every cohort analysis has three main components: the definition of the cohort, the time series over which it is tracked, and an aggregate measure that captures actions taken by cohort members. *Cohort grouping* is frequently anchored to a starting event such as the date a shopper first placed an order, the day a patient began a treatment plan, or the moment a user downloaded an app. Cohorts can also be defined by other attributes, either fixed or variable. Fixed traits include year of birth, country of origin, or the founding year of a company. Variable traits might include current city or employment status. When using changing attributes, it is essential to assign cohorts based on the value at the starting point, since allowing entities to shift between groups over time undermines the analysis. ::: {.callout-note icon="false"} # Expand Your Knowledge **Cohort or Segment?** Although the terms are often used interchangeably, it is helpful to distinguish them. A *cohort* is a set of users (or other entities) who share a common starting date and are observed across time. A *segment* is a grouping of users who share a characteristic at a single point in time, regardless of when they began. Like cohorts, segments can be based on inherent traits such as age or on behavioral factors. For example, users who sign up in the same month can form a cohort that is tracked longitudinally. Segments can also be analyzed with cohort methods to identify which groups exhibit the most valuable behaviors. The analyses in this chapter, including retention, will help tie concrete data to marketing segments. ::: The second element of any cohort analysis is the *time series*. This refers to the chronological record of actions such as purchases, logins, or other interactions completed by the entities under study. For the analysis to be meaningful, the time series must span the full duration of each entity’s activity. If it does not, *survivorship bias* can distort results. Survivorship bias occurs when only those who remain active are included while individuals who have left are missing, which can make the remaining group appear stronger or more loyal than newer cohorts. It is also important that the time series be long enough to capture the behavior of interest. If users typically engage weekly, several weeks of data are needed. If they act only once per year, multiple years of data are required. Because newer cohorts have had less time to perform actions than older ones, cohort analysis usually tracks elapsed periods from the starting point rather than calendar months. This allows comparisons across cohorts at period 1, period 2, and so on, regardless of the actual calendar date. These intervals can be defined as days, weeks, months, or years. The *aggregate metric* should reflect behaviors that are central to the organization’s goals, such as continued product usage or repeat purchases. Metrics are typically aggregated across the cohort using functions such as `sum`, `count`, or `mean`, although other aggregations may be appropriate depending on the context. The resulting time series provides a clear view of how behaviors shift over time. In this chapter, we will examine four key types of cohort analysis: retention, survivorship, returnship (repeat behavior), and cumulative measures. **Retention** Retention focuses on whether a cohort member appears in the time series at a particular point, measured in periods since the starting date. This is especially useful when repeated engagement is expected, such as in streaming media, mobile apps, or subscription services. Retention helps assess how engaging a product is and how many members are likely to remain active in the future. **Survivorship** Survivorship examines how many entities remain in the dataset for a specified duration, regardless of how often they act during that time. This analysis helps estimate the proportion of a population that continues to exist in the system. A persistent entity may be positive, such as a customer who has not churned, or negative, such as a participant who has not completed required milestones. **Returnship** Returnship, or repeat behavior analysis, evaluates whether an action occurs more than a minimum threshold, often more than once, within a defined time window. This is valuable in contexts where behavior is irregular, such as hospitality or retail. It highlights the proportion of customers who return for additional purchases or visits within the selected period. **Cumulative** Cumulative measures capture the total number or value of actions within one or more fixed windows, regardless of when those actions occur. These calculations are often used to estimate customer lifetime value (LTV or CLTV). Together, these four approaches allow us to compare cohorts and uncover differences in their long-term trajectories. They support better decisions in product design, marketing, and financial planning. Since the calculations share a common structure, we will begin with retention and then adapt the same framework to the other types. Before moving into the construction of these analyses, we will first review the dataset that will serve as our running example in this chapter. ## The Online Retail Store Dataset The Polars examples in this chapter use a dataset of sales transactions from a UK online retail store. It contains online transactions recorded between 01/12/2010 and 09/12/2011. The data can be downloaded from the [UC Irvine Machine Learning Repository](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/352/online+retail). @tbl-data-dict-online-retail lists each column in the dataset and provides a brief description of its meaning. | Variable Name | Description | |:---------------|:-------------------------------------------------------| | Invoice_No | A 6-digit integral number uniquely assigned to each transaction. If this code | | | starts with letter 'c', it indicates a cancellation | | Stock_Code | A 5-digit integral number uniquely assigned to each distinct product | | Description | Product name | | Quantity | The quantities of each product (item) per transaction | | Invoice_Date | The day and time when each transaction was generated | | Unit_Price | Product price per unit | | Customer_ID | A 5-digit integral number uniquely assigned to each customer | | Country | The name of the country where each customer resides | : Data dictionary for the online retail store dataset. {#tbl-data-dict-online-retail} With a clear understanding of cohort analysis and the dataset used throughout the chapter, we can now look at how to write Polars code for retention analysis. The central question is how long customers remain active after they are acquired. ## Retention Among the different forms of cohort analysis, *retention analysis* is one of the most widely used. Retention refers to the ability to hold on to something over time. Skills, for example, must be practiced regularly to avoid decline. In business, keeping existing customers engaged is often more valuable than acquiring new ones because loyal customers tend to generate higher long-term profits. Organizations also strive to retain employees, since hiring and training replacements requires significant time and resources. The central focus of retention analysis is whether the initial size of a cohort, such as the number of users, employees, or total spending, remains stable, decreases, or grows as time passes. When it changes, both the magnitude and the rate of that change matter. Cohorts usually shrink over time because once a group is defined, new members cannot be added. Revenue, however, may follow a different pattern. Even if some customers leave, those who remain might increase their spending in later months. Retention analysis measures either the `count` of participants or the `sum` of money or actions across each period beginning with the cohort’s creation. These values are normalized by dividing them by the initial figure to produce percentages. The first period always equals 100 percent. Over time, retention based on counts inevitably declines and cannot exceed 100 percent. In contrast, retention based on spending or actions may rise above 100 percent if activity increases. Results are commonly shown in tables or graphs known as retention curves. Later in this chapter, several examples of these curves will be introduced. Retention curves allow comparisons between cohorts. One key feature to examine is the early portion of the curve, which often shows a steep decline. For many consumer apps, it is common for half the users to become inactive within the first few months. If one cohort’s curve is noticeably steeper or flatter than another, it may point to differences in product design or acquisition channels worth further analysis. It is also helpful to observe whether the curve levels off or continues to fall toward zero. A plateau suggests that the remaining members are likely to stay engaged for the long term. In some cases, curves bend upward when users return after a period of inactivity, creating what is sometimes called a smile curve. For subscription-based businesses, revenue-focused curves are especially important because rising revenue per customer over time indicates a strong and sustainable SaaS model. This section will guide you through building a retention analysis, incorporating cohort groupings from time series data, and addressing gaps or sparsity in the dataset. With this foundation, the next section will show how to adapt the approach for other types of cohort analysis. Because retention is the most detailed example, this part of the chapter will be the most extensive, helping you develop both the code and the intuition needed for the calculations involved. ### Polars for a Basic Retention Curve When conducting retention analysis, similar to other cohort studies, three elements are essential: how the cohort is defined, a timeline of user actions, and an aggregate metric that reflects an important business outcome or process. In our case, the cohorts consist of individual customers, the timeline measures how long it takes each one to make a repeat purchase, and the key measure is the number of customers who continue buying from the online store during each period after the initial date. The first step is to load the dataset and review its descriptive statistics to confirm that the main columns do not contain missing values. ::: {#c5d90bf8 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import polars as pl online_retail = pl.read_excel('data/uk_online_retail_sales.xlsx') (online_retail .select(pl.exclude('Description','StockCode')) .describe() ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}

At the same time, we will add a helper function that converts column names from *PascalCase* into a specialized form of *Snake_Case* for consistent naming throughout the book. ::: {#50342630 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} def pascal_to_snake(name: str) -> str: out = [] for i, ch in enumerate(name): if ( ch.isupper() and i > 0 and not name[i-1].isupper() ): out.append('_') out.append(ch) return ''.join(out) online_retail_clean = (online_retail .filter(pl.col('InvoiceNo').is_not_null(), pl.col('CustomerID').is_not_null()) .rename(pascal_to_snake) ) ``` ::: With the dataset cleaned, we can begin building a simple retention calculation before moving to more detailed cohort breakdowns. The first task is to identify the earliest purchase date for each customer, stored as *First_Purchase*. This value serves as the baseline for measuring how many periods pass before subsequent transactions. To obtain it, compute the `min` *Invoice_Date* for every *Customer_ID* using `over`, which uniquely identifies each customer. ::: {#ab00ddc1 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} (online_retail_clean .with_columns(pl.col('Invoice_Date').dt.date()) .with_columns(First_Purchase=pl.min('Invoice_Date').over('Customer_ID')) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}

While shorter intervals could be used, the dataset shows limited variation at hourly or daily levels. The number of customers with activity in each interval represents the retained population for that period. ::: {#c7d80e0e .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} (online_retail_clean .with_columns(pl.col('Invoice_Date').dt.date()) .with_columns(First_Purchase=pl.min('Invoice_Date').over('Customer_ID')) .with_columns(Period=(pl.col('Invoice_Date').sub('First_Purchase')).dt.total_days() // 7) .group_by('Period') .agg(Cohort_Retained=pl.col('Customer_ID').n_unique()) .sort('Period') ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}

This makes it possible to divide *Cohort_Retained* by the cohort size. The `first` function retrieves the initial record, and when used with `over`, it selects the first entry based on the column provided in `sort`. In this example, the *Cohort_Size* comes directly from the very first record in the dataset, so the `over` clause is not needed: ::: {#2e520418 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} import polars_permute to_plot = (online_retail_clean .with_columns(pl.col('Invoice_Date').dt.date()) .with_columns(First_Purchase=pl.min('Invoice_Date').over('Customer_ID')) .with_columns(Period=(pl.col('Invoice_Date').sub('First_Purchase')).dt.total_days() // 7) .group_by('Period') .agg(Cohort_Retained=pl.col('Customer_ID').n_unique()) .sort('Period') .with_columns(Cohort_Size=pl.col('Cohort_Retained').first()) .with_columns(Pct_Retained=pl.col('Cohort_Retained') / pl.col('Cohort_Size')) .permute.swap('Cohort_Retained','Cohort_Size') # <1> ) to_plot ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
